Package org.aeonbits.owner.loaders

Class DotEnvLoader

java.lang.Object
org.aeonbits.owner.loaders.DotEnvLoader
All Implemented Interfaces:
Serializable, Loader
public class DotEnvLoader extends Object implements Loader
A loader able to read a .env file, the format that container tooling has made the commonest way to carry configuration into a process.

The file is a list of NAME=value lines. Blank lines are skipped and a line whose first non-blank character is # is a comment. Everything beyond that — whether quotes delimit a value or belong to it, whether \n means a newline, whether a comment may follow a value on the same line — differs from one tool to the next, because .env has no specification. Those differences are described by an EnvDialect, and the default is EnvDialect.DOCKER, which does nothing at all to a value.

The dialect can be chosen in two ways. Registering the loader sets it for a factory:

     ConfigFactory.registerLoader(new DotEnvLoader(EnvDialect.DOTENV));

and an option on the source sets it for that file alone, which is finer:

     @Sources("file:.env#dialect=dotenv")

The options of a source live in the fragment, for every loader and every scheme - see SourceOptions. They may also adjust one rule at a time, over the dialect or over the default: quotes=strip|literal, escapes=expand|literal, export=strip|keep, comments=inline|none, multiline=allow|deny, continuation=allow|deny and bare=env|ignore|error, separated by &. An option or a setting that is not one of these is refused rather than ignored.

This loader accepts any source whose path ends in .env, which covers both a file that is all extension and one such as local.env. It contributes nothing to the sources that are looked for when an interface carries no @Sources: a .env is seldom on the classpath and is never named after the configuration interface, so it is always named explicitly.

Under a dialect that keeps quotes — the default — a value written NAME="Matteo" almost certainly came from a file meant for dotenv. Reading it verbatim is right but silent, so one WARNING per file is written through java.util.logging, which is part of the JDK: OWNER adds no logging dependency. Choosing the dialect that fits the file is the real cure; failing that, the message is silenced with org.aeonbits.owner.loaders.DotEnvLoader.level = OFF in a logging.properties, or with Logger.getLogger(DotEnvLoader.class.getName()).setLevel(Level.OFF). Logger names are a hierarchy, so org.aeonbits.owner.level = OFF quietens the whole library.

    • defaultSpecFor

      public String defaultSpecFor(String uriPrefix)
      Returns the default URI specification for a given URI resource, that can be handled by this loader.

      Returning null means this loader adds nothing to the sources looked for in the absence of @Sources - which is what SystemLoader and DotEnvLoader both do, since neither is named after the configuration interface. That is also why this method has a default: it is a choice a loader is allowed to decline, and declining it should not require writing a method that returns nothing.

      A loader offering more than one name - a format spelled .yaml and .yml, or .ini and .cfg - overrides Loader.defaultSpecsFor(String) instead. The two are not meant to be overridden together.

      Always null: a .env file is not named after the configuration interface, so there is no useful name to guess, and returning nothing keeps this loader from adding a lookup to every configuration that is loaded.

      Specified by:
      defaultSpecFor in interface Loader
      Parameters:
      uriPrefix - the prefix identifying the URI resource.
      Returns:
      the default URI specification for a given URI resource, or null for none.
